LUNAR DAYS AND EIGHTEEN-MONTHS
PHENOMENAL EXTREMES OF HEAT AND COLD.

Dr. Klein, German astronomer, has recently called the attention of sometimes to lunar crater, some three miles wide, which had not before been observed, and which he feels surely was not in existence two years ago. Astronomers have long since given up all hope of tracing either the signs of actual life upon the moon or traces of the past existence of living creatures there. But there are still among them those who believe that by sedulous and careful scientific processes of material change may be recognized in that seemingly inert mass. In reality, perhaps the wonder rather is that signs of change should not be often recognized, than that from time to time new craters should appear or the walls of old craters fall in. The moon's surface is exposed to variations of temperature compared with which those affecting the surface of our earth are altogether trifling. It is true there is no summer or winter on the moon.

Sir W. Herschel has spoken of the lunar seasons as though they resemble our own, but in reality they are very different. The sun's midday height at any lunar station is only about three degrees greater in summer than in winter, whereas our summer sun is forty-seven degrees higher in the sky at noon than our winter sun. In fact, midsummer's day on the moon does not differ more from midwinter's day, as far as the sun's actual path on the sky is concerned, than as the 18th of March differs from the 25th, or the 18th of September from the 9th. It is the change from day to night which chiefly affects the moon's surface in the lunar year of seasons; lasting 402 of our days, each lasting twenty-nine and three-quarters of ours. Thus day lasts more than a fortnight, and is followed by a night of equal length. Nor is this all. There is neither air nor moisture to produce such effects as are produced by our air and the moisture it contains in mitigating the heat of day and cold of night. Under the sun's rays the moon's surface becomes hotter and hotter as the long lunar day proceeds, until its heat exceeds that of boiling water; but so soon as the sun has set the heat thus received is rapidly radiated away into space (no screen of moisture-laden air checking its escape), and long before lunar midnight cold exists compared with which the bitterest weather ever experienced by Arctic voyagers would be oppressively hot.

These are not merely theoretical conclusions, though even as such they could be thoroughly relied upon. The moon's heat has been measured by the present Lord Rosse (using his father's splendid six-foot mirror). He separated the heat which the moon simply reflects to us from that which her heated surface herself gives out; for, technically, he separated the reflected from the radiated heat by using a glass screen which allowed the former heat to pass while it intercepted the latter. He thus found about six-sevenths of the heat we receive from the moon is due to the heating of her own substance. From the entire series of observations it appeared that the change of temperature during the entire lunar day—that is, from near midnight to near midday on the moon—amounts to fully 500 degrees Fahrenheit, &c. We assume that the cold at lunar midnight corresponds with about 50 degrees below zero (the greatest cold experienced in Arctic travelling has never exceeded 140 degrees below zero), it would follow that the midday heat was considerably greater than that of boiling water on the earth at the sea level. But the range of change is not a matter for depreciation. It certainly amounts to about 800 degrees, and in whatever way we distribute it, we must admit first, that no such life as we are familiar with could possibly exist on the moon; and secondly, that the moon's crust must possess a life of its own, so to speak, expanding and contracting increasingly and energetically.—London Times.

This contraction, says the advocate of the resumption act, was necessary in order to resume specie payments on January 1, 1879. But it is one thing to begin specie payment and another to continue it. Very probably the Secretary of the Treasury can begin specie payment on January 1, but the question remains, could such specie payment be maintained? France has more metallic than paper money, and they can easily maintain specie payment; but the United States has at least three dollars in paper to one in coin, and while this disproportion exists, even little war, or a change in the balance of trade might make shipwreck of their pretended specie payment.

EXPENDITURES.

The last fiscal year of Democratic administration was that ending June 30, 1860. The ordinary expenses of the government for that year exclusive of pensions and interest on the public debt were $58,055,652. Under Republican rule, for the year ending June 30, 1875, the same expenses were $142,073,632, or nearly two and one-half times as great as under Democratic rule in 1860. Our population was 31,443,321, expenditures $18.71 per capita; in 1876, the population, as near as it can be estimated, was 43,000,000; expenditures per capita so much less. These comparisons are based upon ordinary government expenses in time of peace, and no expenditures incident to or arising from the war have been included in the figures given. Taking the seven fiscal years, from 1854 to 1860 inclusive, under Democratic administration, the expenditures per capita were $18 in the seven years; from 1869 to 1875 inclusive, under Republican rule, they were $30.

CORRUPTION.

It is not necessary to speak in detail of the corruption which has brought disgrace upon the Republic, and furnished despots the world over, with arguments against popular government. A bare reference brings them forth: Credit Mobilier, Pacific Mail, Bankrupt, Custom house villainies, post office straw bids, the Indian and whisky rings, and the long list of defaulters in every department.

HIS FRAUDULENCY.

There is one great drama of fraud, one huge black spot upon the national escutcheon, that cannot be passed by with a mere allusion. The seat of the Chief Magistrate is occupied by a man who was never elected and whose elevation was accomplished by the grossest frauds and boldest usurpations that ever disgraced the history of free people. Though the erroneous decision by which Congress counted in Hayes and Wheeler may not be reversible, that fact only makes it the decision and the means by which it was brought about.

If the people ever condone this great sin, if they ever pardon the guilty men who perpetrated it—and nearly every one of whom has been rewarded by office under the administration—the most sanguine advocate of popular government will have reason to hang his head in shame, and doubt the possibility of its success.

Yes, my fellow-citizens, the very existence of government, if it is possible to maintain it, and to maintain its purity, is now on trial before you. As you love the institutions bequeathed to you by the fathers, as you reverence your constitution and value your freedom, as you esteem virtue and detest all wickedness, you are bound, in no uncertain tones, to manifest your abhorrence of the great usurpation, SECTIONALISM.

Another great topic remains to be considered, and when I shall have offered some brief observations upon it, my task will be done. It is thirteen years since the close of the war, thirteen years since a hand was raised or word spoken against the preservation of the Union, and yet articles are now written, and speeches are now made by men, prominent in the Republican party, the bitterness of which is scarcely paralleled by anything that was written or said when war was flagrant, and the Union was in danger.

Fellow citizens, nothing more unjust, nothing more unpatriotic, nothing more injurious to the peace, welfare and prosperity of the republic, nothing more clearly demonstrative of the necessity for change of rulers, and the inauguration of an era of justice and fraternity, than is afforded by these facts, can be imagined.

Do you wish the Union preserved? Then support those who would bind it together by the ties of fraternal feeling and common interest, as well as by constitutions and laws. A BUSY TIME FOR BENCH AND BAR.
RENEWAL OF ACTIVITY IN THE COURTS—LONG CALENDARS.

Saturday marked the close of the lawyers' vacation. To-day all the Civil Courts begin the regular routine of trials. The increase in the calendars has been very large. Judges Davis and Brady of the Supreme Court have returned from their vacation to hold, with Judge Ingalls, the general term. The calendar has on it over 300 cases, the largest number yet reached. The circuit calendar has on it about 500 cases, an increase of 100 last October. There are to be three circuit terms; Judges Donohue, Lawrence and Van Brunt sitting them, with the possibility that Judges Donohue and Barrett will exchange for part of the month, during which Judge Barrett is assigned to chambers. Judge Worst will sit special term, which has had 200 notices added to it. The Court of oyer and terminer will be held either by Judge Barrett or Judge Donohue.

The Superior Court has general term this month, but three trial terms to be presided over by Judges Speer, Curtis and Sedgwick, while Judge Freedah will hold the special. The Common Pleas has no general term; Chief Justice Daly and Judge Lawrence will hold chambers, and the equity will be held by Judges Robinson and J. R. Daly. The Marine Court will hold its usual terms.

The most interesting business likely to come before the Courts early this working season is that growing out of the elevated railways and out of the city disputes with the Brooklyn Bridge Company and with taxpayers.

There will be two branches of the Court of Sessions this month to be held by Recorder Hackett and Judge Gidderseye.

same time there was a very general
feeling in favor of abstaining from it,
and hence perhaps it came that sec
ond marriage was from the first pro-
hibited to them. The council of Nice
refused to impose any absolute rule of
celibacy on the priesthood, but in the
fourth century these marriages had
come to be looked upon as unlawful,
though not invalid, in the west, and a
decree of Pope Siricius in 385—the
first authentic Papal decretal on rec
ord—peremptorily interdicts it. The
ultimate moral results of this ordinance
were, to say the least, of very mixed
kind. The state of clerical morality in
the ninth and tenth centuries is on-
ly too notorious. In the tenth century
Ratherius, an Italian bishop, said that
if he were to enforce the canons against
unchaste persons administering eccles-
iastical rites there would be no one left
in the church except boys, and if he en-
forced the canons against bastards they
also must be excluded. With the
eleventh century came the great reform
of Hildebrand, who has hardly had
justice done to him in this respect by
the generality of modern critics. No
doubt in making clerical marriages not
only illegal but invalid, and even taking
the unprecedented step of appealing to
the people and bidding them refuse the
ministry of married priests, he was
ruthlessly enforcing hard and infexi-
ble discipline. But it must be remem-
bered that the existing condition of
things was simply appalling; that no
body in that age thought of seriously
proposing the abolition of compulsory
celibacy, though nearly everybody
claimed the right to evade it; and,
moreover, that in the feudal state of
society there was a very real and press
ing danger of ecclesiastical benefices
becoming hereditary, like lay fiefs, if
the marriage or tolerated concubinage
of the clergy was left to continue un-
checked; and the priesthood would
then have sunk to the moral and intel-
lectual level of the rude and ignorant
chiefs by whom they were surrounded.
It is difficult to see what other line an
earnest and energetic reformer in Hilde-
brand's position could have taken,
though it by no means follows that
what was the best or only practicable
remedy for the disorders of the eleventh
century is therefore suitable for all
ages, especially with the light thrown
upon it by the accumulated experience
of eight more centuries since. That
light is a lucid one. The canons of
medieval councils and the writings of
medieval saints bristle with denuncia-
tions of the prevalent immorality of
the clergy, from which the court of
Rome was very far from being generally
exempt. It became customary in
many countries for the laity to insist,
as a precautionary measure, on their
pastor taking a concubine, and the
same usage is said to prevail in some
places now. In 1522 this practice of
the laity was expressly condemned in a
canon of Spanish provincial council;
Nicholas de Clomangis at the council of
Constance declared it to be very com-
mon, adding that nobody believed in
the real observance of celibate vows,
and those who were not chargeable with
concubinage were accordingly credited
with worse vices. His language is too
strikingly explicit to bear reproduction
here, even in what Gibbon calls the
"decent obscurity of a learned language."
Sarpi, in his History of the council of
Trent, speaks of the same custom as
then prevailing in Switzerland,
and much the same is said in
our own day in Spain, and still more
of South America.

The majority of the Senate committee on Military Affairs, to-day authorized Senator Cockrell to report the House bill, placing General James Shields on the retired list of the army, favorably and without amendment. The report for the year ending Dec. 31, 1877, shows that 3,042 miles of road are in operation; gross earnings for the year $2,473,203.56; operating expenses, $527,342.90; a decrease in gross earnings of $585,655 against last year. Clark of Omaha; John Sharp of Salt Lake City; G. N. Dodge of Council Bluffs and W. A. H. Loveland of Colorado.

quite evident that the evils of the law had
become so apparent as to be no longer JUS
ti6abie by any argument which could be
brought to bear on the question. The
real aim of bankrupt law should be to
afford honest but unfortunate men an
opportunity to be released from their obi
cations Of indebtedness upon surrender Of
all assets in their possession. In the case
Of the law just repealed the legal proceed
ings generally eat up the assets. and fraud
uleut evasions let the dishonest debtor
escape with enough to start anew, and free
from his creditors.


A national bankrupt law would be much
preferable in our judgment to State bank
rupt laws, and Congress ought now to
frame a law which should be just and
equitable in its provisions, and protect
both creditor and debtor class.

doubtedly be Of benefit to the country,
though such an one as that just repealed
is worse than none.

From the Indianapolis Times, August 11.

New York, August 8, 1878.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE INDIANAPOLIS TIMES:—
COMRADE LIGHT:—
MY DEAR FRIEND—Your kind letter OF 25th July duly in hand. I feel gratified at the fact that you have determined to hold labor demonstration at Indianapolis and deeply regret that circumstances prevent my being present. We have little to hope from the rule OF the capitalist CLASS; which, at present, conducts the affairs OF the nation, and we must never forget that "the emancipation OF the workers must be achieved by the workers themselves." We may truly congratulate the socialistic labor party upon the success with which it has forced upon the people a recognition OF the labor question and thus made it a national question. Nay, a question OF universal importance. The present unhappy CONDITION OF the laborer in the United States finds its parallel in almost every country due TO the cupidity and ignorance OF rulers. The object OF the socialistic labor party is to place government upon scientific basis; and to that end radical change in the personnel OF the government is an imperative necessity. This measure may be accomplished by the ballot. It is then necessary to obtain disse the knowledge necessary to the complete achievement OF the above aim. This measure can be accomplished only by study and education. From this it would follow that the socialistic labor party must be both party OF action and party OF education. The question OF its immediate or remote success will be answered by the intelligence and vigor with which members impel it toward the performance of this twofold function. Seeing that our brothers of Indianapolis are so nobly working toward these noble ends, I send them, through you, my heartfelt sympathy and most sincere congratulations. Tell them to fearlessly unfurl the red flag, to march heart to heart for it is the only symbol which represents the universal brotherhood of labor—peace, love, justice and science—of which it is the emblem. Tell them to defend it as they would defend the honor which it symbolizes—the honor OF humanity. Truly yours in the holy Cause OF labor,

JUSTUS H. SCHWAB.

1t is well known fact that from time
immemoriai herds of wild horses have
roamed over the plains of southwestern
Kansas. Their origin no man knoweth.
1t may be dated back 10 the early Span
ish conquest of the country. It has
been exceedingly difficult to capture
them, the method pursued having been
to run down and lasso them with feet
horses. Latterly, however, it is found
that they can be captured in herds. The
method is to get up an outfit of fast
walking team on wagon carrying pro-
visions and camp supplies, and three or
four riding ponies, and as many men.
When herd is found they are kept
moving, no effort being made to drive
them in any direction. The teams and
ponies are not driven faster than a walk
and every opportunity is embraced of
cutting across to save distance. The
wild horses are kept in motion till dark,
being given no opportunity to Craze
during the day. At night they are too
tired to Craze and will lie down. The
pursuers camp, feed their horses from
grain which they carry with them and
are up by daylight, have breakfast and
start again. This is kept up every day.
Every day takes some of the scare and
wild out of them; they become accus-
toned to the sight of the men on horse
back and the team find they are not
going to be hurt by them, and, tired and
leg weary with constant travel and little
feed, and in from eight to ten days will
allow the men to ride in among them and
drive them in any direction. They are
then headed for the ranch and are quite
tame and docile by the time they get
in. They are of the pony order, such as
used in the cattle business, make good
riding ponies, and when thoroughly
broken, good teams for light driving in
that country. They sell, when broken
to ride, at SIS to $25 per head, and when
broken to drive at from $50 to $75 per
span.

The surplus OF the National banks amounted on October nearly $19,900,900. Part OF this sum represents the profits earned by former State banks previous to their conversion into National organizations, and brought by them into the system. The greater portion was, however, accumulated by banks during the years of business prosperity immediately succeeding the close OF the war. The table given, showing that the maximum surplus reached in 1878, when it was $18,881,690, since which time it has been decreased to $5,151,000. The losses in 1876, $1,971,900; in 1877, $1,188,558; in 1878, $2,466,800; total $6,419,415. The report continues:


The greater portion OF the losses mentioned has been cancelled by charging it TO the account of current profits, in consequence OF which 351 banks in the last six months paid no dividends at all; banks semi-annually passing dividends on account of loss had 255. This number is equal to about one-seventh OF the whole number now in operation.


The average amount OF capital upon which no dividends have been paid during that time is $14,353,000. More than one-tenth OF the total capital OF the National banks has been without profit to the shareholders.


The belief so widely entertained that the profits made by the National banks are excessive, is in great part due TO the exceptionally large dividends paid by a few banks which are temporarily located and have large surplus and which make large returns TO their shareholders on the amount OF their nominal capital. The profits OF these banks are not to a considerable extent derived from interest, but from surplus and deposits. Many the banks making exceptional dividends have much less amount OF circulation than those making moderate dividends only, while a few of them have no circulation whatever.

The estimated losses are only $6,511,423. Mr. Knox says the average number of failures during each OF the past fifteen years is less than 10, and the average annual loss less than $4,000.

One OF the chief objects in the organization OF the National system, not only to furnish bank notes which were safe and convertible, but supply a steady market for and facilitate the negotiation OF United States bonds, and is doubt that the credit OF the Government and its ability To borrow money at low interest bonds has for the National bank notes.

From the New York Times


Christmas At Windsor Castle.


A GLIMPSE OF THE PRIVATE LIFE OF MONARCH
How THE QUEEN AND HER CHILDREN HUNG UP THEIR STOCKINGS—A Rich DESCRIPTION


It is rarely that the public obtains a glimpse of the private life of monarchs.


They are never seen by their subjects except in full dress, and equipped with what New England people are accustomed to call "company manners." Thus only the outer shell, so to speak, of the German Emperor or the British Queen is known to their people. We all know, of course, that the Emperor is mortal, and hence must at times be put in night-shirt, and that even Queen Victoria must do up her back hair on going to bed, just as though she were an ordinary British matron, but even the most enterprising special correspondent is unable to describe those imperial and royal acts from his own personal knowledge. We of this generation are, however, exceptionally fortunate in regard to the good and gracious Queen of England. In the Life of The Prince Consort, which is virtually written by her, we are taken into the interior of the royal palace and admitted to the privacy of the royal family. It is safe to say that the present generation is acquainted with the royal family of England more intimately than any previous generation has been acquainted with any other royal household. The Queen's description of Christmas at Windsor Castle is of especial interest just at present, and as it has not yet been published, a summary of it, obtained from advance sheets, may interest the readers of the Times.


The occasion was that of the year 1849. Especial efforts were made to render that occasion one of unusual domestic felicity. The Prince Consort said, "Mother, we must have first-class things for the children this time," and the amiable Queen had answered, "Albert, we will just make things whoop." Accordingly an immense amount of presents was provided, and the royal parents determined to personally superintend the filling of the stockings—a duty which ordinarily devolved upon Lord John Russell. "On Christmas eve," we are told, "the Queen remarked, 'Albert, I believe I will hang up my own stocking, and you shall fill it.' The Prince, with that excellent good sense which never failed him, replied, 'My dear, it will not do. There must be a limit to the size of stockings. Hang up a pillowcase, if you want to, or even a bolster, but remember that I cannot afford to sit up all night filling unlimited space with expensive presents.'" Her Majesty thereupon changed her mind, and, full of anxiety to make her husband happy, volunteered to fill the stockings herself, so that the Prince could go to bed early. During the evening the children were of course unusually wide awake. Half a dozen times was the Queen compelled to go to the foot of the front stairs and order them to go instantly to sleep. Threats were even necessary before they could be quieted, and the Prince Consort was finally obliged to remark, "If you children let me hear one more word out of you this night, I shall come upstairs with a club." Whereupon the children ceased their uproar and by 10 o'clock were soundly asleep.


It was the wish of the Prince, continues the narrative, "to sleep in the nursery with the children, so that he could see them open their stockings in the morning." As the Queen desired to hang a portrait of herself over the Prince's bed, to his pleasant surprise, she was compelled to wait until he was sound asleep. At 1 o'clock A.M., Her Majesty stealthily entered the nursery with some well-filled stockings hanging on her arm. Just as she crossed the threshold two of the stockings slipped from her grasp and fell with considerable noise, but without awakening the children or interrupting Prince Albert's gentle snore. It so happened that the Duke of Wellington had, when filling the stove for the night, inadvertently left a coal-scuttle in the middle of the floor, and the Queen, not dreaming of such an obstacle, fell over it with a loud crash. The Prince of Wales moved uneasily in his bed, but continued to sleep soundly as did all the other children and their numerous gatherers. Fortunately the Queen fell on the stockings which were merely stuffed with messiness, candy of a Wellington nature, and so sustained no injury. Finally the stockings were hung in their proper place and the Queen proceeded to place her portrait on the wall over the Prince Consort's head. To do this it was necessary for her to stand on the bed. Now, to walk over a well-filled bed in a dim-lit room is a difficult question, and it seems she stumbled that in an attempt to stand heavily upon the Prince. It was the last step that broke her princely slumber and also flattened his ribs. In those moments instead of bringing him peace, she merely pressed heavily and exclaimed so on in a manner that in the midst of them set Princess of Cambridge in alarm, yet she could not be unalarmed. Further on that effect, as many wish Her Majesty had this misfortune and further, her heart burst into tears and nearly fell upon her, thereby eliciting a cry of terror from the children who, fearing that terror had arrived, startled from their sleep and arrived quite startled from their sleeping, and began to cry, which is common in the blessed Christmas time.

May Frank take as much comfort with his girl as we do with the cigars.

The nationals favor the reduction of saloon license. Their argument is that it will not decrease the city's revenue from this source, as it is only a question whether we shall have 20 saloons at $500 or 80 at $500. The saloon keepers are not all of the same mind on this subject, some of them being willing to pay $1,000 and thereby freeze a large portion of the small dealers out.

And now another railroad enterprise, calling itself the Banner Coal Co., asks for right of way across Rock River bridge and along the highway. The council cannot well refuse this company since they have granted the right to the Marrow Gauge Co., without making a monopoly of the interest of the latter. The prevailing opinion among business men, however, is that, inasmuch as that bridge was purchased and repaired by the city for the especial purpose of affording an inlet to the city from the farming community south of the river, it should preserve the bridge to that purpose; or if a railroad company must have it, let them buy it and run it at their own expense.

The Boy Nuisance.

Boys ranging from 8 to 15 years of age have made themselves a nuisance in this city and particularly about the T. P. & W. depot, by committing innumerable petit depredations, using loud and obscene language, scuffing on the platform, meddling with freight and baggage and doing many annoyances. Mr. Hines, station agent, borne with them, demonstrated against such conduct and in friendly and kind manner told them to keep away from the depot time after time, until last Tuesday, when their conduct was such that he considered there was no more virtue in forbearance and that the interference of law would have to be invoked. He accordingly placed in the hands of the Marshal a list of the names of eighteen of the often offenders whom he made complaint before Magistrate Grover. This morning six of them were caught and brought up for trial, viz. Douglas Barker, Fred Wells, Eddie Seder, Chas. Johnson, Albert and Ben Larson.

The specific charge was that, on Tuesday of last week they had maliciously damaged a lot of paper-rags which were lying on the depot platform by throwing them at each other and about the platform, thereby bursting the sacks and scattering the rags and continuing to do so after having been warned to desist. Besides this there was a general charge of continuous mischief and general deviltry. Young Barker was fined $5 and costs. Fred Wells, who was not proven to have participated in the scrape, but plead guilty to the general charge, was fined $1 and costs. Eddie Seder's fine was $5, which he induced his mother to pay after some hard pleading and extravagant promises. Albert and Ben Larson, two very hard looking captives for boys of their ages—10 to 11 years—were fined $1 and costs each, being suspended during good behavior. Lieu Chas. Johnson, son of Sack Olaf, was charged $5 and costs for his share of the sport, notwithstanding the fact that his father swore the boy was at home sick at the time of the rag affair.

When the others are caught they should be proportionately punished, if the fine of this kind of boys can be called punishment, and a stop put to such ruffians. The fact is that fining a boy and making his father pay the fine is no punishment to the boys and will result in very little good. The twenty-four hours confinement in a calaboose would be more effectual than a dozen such fines as the above.

Special Dispatch to the Register.

The question which has so long occupied the public mind as to what man should fill the place made vacant when the Senator Matthews' time expires, has at last been settled and Hon. George F. Pendleton, of Cincinnati, has been chosen. The subject has been the theme of conversation in city, town and hamlet, since the late October election when the Democrats gained control of the State. Mr. Pendleton had to contend with two men of more than ordinary popularity from the start—General Ewing, the man of inflation ideas, and General George W. Morgan, who was also an anti resumptionist, but not of an extremist to the extent that Ewing was. Ten days since it was most generally conceded that Pendleton and Ewing were about even, with possibility of the former leading on the first ballot; Ewing counted his followers that could be relied upon at thirty, while General Morgan was credited with following of about twenty. Of late few other candidates came in the field, Hurd of Toledo, and Payne of Cleveland. The ballots show how weak was their strength. During the past week all of these candidates have been in the city, with large lobbies working for their interests. Up to last night there were few who did not concede that Pendleton would have a tight fight if he won the honors. Yesterday, however, a most scurrilous attack was made upon Pendleton in the shape of a circular. At first it created confusion, but last night his friends had recovered, and it was found that, instead of causing a break in the ranks, it had only served to strengthen them by adding men who were before doubtful as to who they would support. As predicted last night, Pendleton gained during the day. From this cause alone it was charged that Ewing or his hackers were at the bottom of the onslaught. The effect was that many of Ewing's men deserted him. He fell off at least ten in the first ballot from the number conceded him by the other candidates. See ballot. During the balloting Mr. Pendleton remained at his room at the Neil House, while Generals Ewing and Morgan occupied quarters in the State House.

The caucus was held in secret session, no reporter being able to gain admission, not even the clerks of Senate were allowed admission.

At the close of the second ballot the Ewing men moved for an adjournment but this was most emphatically voted down. During the balloting the halls and corridors were densely packed.

At an early hour this morning a very powerful delegation arrived from Cincinnati, and reinforced the almost worn out defenders of Pendleton. They worked like troopers during the day, and the fight has been extremely bitter during the past twenty-four hours. After the third ballot was announced, and it was known that Pendleton was elected there was a rush for his hotel where he was warmly congratulated. A speech was called for when the whole body adjourned to the Hall of the House of Representatives where speeches were delivered by Messrs. Pendleton, Ewing and Morgan. Mr. Pendleton thanked all those who had supported him in this contest, and said he was proud to think there had been no ill feeling among any of the contestants and God helping him, he would do justly to the best of his ability.

W.S.
Associated Press Dispatch.

COLUMBUS, January 10.—The Democratic Joint caucus met tonight, all outsiders and newspaper men being excluded.

The first ballot for Senator resulted as follows: Pendleton 40, Morgan 21, Ewing 11, Ward 8, Hurd 5, Converse 1.

Second ballot resulted: Pendleton 44, Morgan 15, Ewing 20, Ward 4, Payne 1, Converse 1.

At the conclusion of the second ballot a motion was made to adjourn, which was voted down.

The third ballot resulted: Pendleton 81, Ewing 10, Morgan 10, Ward 3, Converse 2, Payne 1. Pendleton was declared the nominee.

During all this time, the contention has been steadily growing worse. But on the sixth ballot, the witches performed their incantation and the climax was reached. When Taylor county was called, the delegation asked permission to retire which was granted. While the convention was waiting for the return of this delegation, Hon. L. Lively, of Lewis county, rose and began to speak. "Why is it that the Democratic convention cannot be conducted with decorum?" he asked. "Why is it that the lowest candidate is not brought up for the purpose of defeating Col. Ben Wilson?" Mr. Geo. O. Davenport, of Ohio county, rose to point out which was that no delegate could make speech while a ballot was being taken. This was all said amid boots, yells, cries of order, "take your seat!" &c. Lively stated he wanted to make a change in the Lewis county vote, in lieu of Wood which had been decided by Wood county delegate. This brought Mr. C. T. Caldwell, of Wood, who said he was the person whom the gentleman from Lewis referred to. The charge that he had tampered with the Lewis county delegation, was also immediately met with a tremendous shout, but Charley was unawed. He was a French warrior who said before a battle, "My children, if you lose sight of our colors, rally to my white plume!" Charley raised high his black hat, in his clenched hand, and began a gallant charge on Ben Wilson, who sat near. He declared, "This gentleman, two years ago, had declared himself not to be a candidate again." And pointing his finger straight at Col. Wilson, who sat pale as a ghost, he declared, "I deny the charge. All the preceding scenes faded into insignificance beside what occurred then, for all at once there was a wild yell, as all the fends from heaven that fell, had peaced the hammer cry of hell!" A thousand excited men were swaying, clanging and yelling. Ben Wilson remained motionless and silent. He said he never has and probably never will deny these charges.

Col. J. B. Killebrew, Commissioner of
Agriculture for Tennessee, writes as follows
upon the above subject:

The impression general that tobacco is
a great exhauster of the soil, especially
among those who know nothing of its culture
of all crops grown in our latitude. We know
at home that impairs the fertility of the soil
so little and the reason is plain. The pro-
cess of reproduction in plants, and ANIMALS,
is a most exhaustive one. The craving
upon the soil is always greatest when the
seeds of plants are allowed to mature.
Corn fodder may be grown in succession
of years upon the same land without any
apparent loss in fertility, but if the ears
are allowed to form and come to maturity
the effect will be quickly seen in the gradual
reduction of the yield. The same may
be said of wheat, hay, cotton, and any other
crop, the seeds of which are allowed to
mature. Now, tobacco ripens no seed;
the seed-bud is pinched out before it can
bloom, and every effort made by the plant
to reproduce is checked. Moreover, the
amount of mineral and organic matter re-
moved from the soil is small when compared
with the potato crop, or even with
good wheat or corn crop. One thousand
pounds of tobacco, after being cured and
stripped, from each acre, would be con-
sidered an excellent crop. The stalks are
afterwards returned to the soil. An acre
in potatoes would yield ten thousand pounds;
three fourths of this is water, leaving two
five hundred pounds dry and mineral
matter. An acre of land that would make
one thousand pounds of tobacco ought to
make twenty-five bushels of wheat, which
would abstract fifteen hundred pounds, i.e.
half more organic and mineral matter
than tobacco. The same land ought to
make forty bushels of corn, or 2,210
pounds more than twice the amount re-
moved by tobacco crop.

Besides these reasons, there is no crop
that completely shades the land as tobacco
does. During the hottest months, when the
power of the sun parches up vegetation, and
exposes the surface to injurious currents,
the broad leaves of tobacco set like an im-
penetrable shield and screen the soil from
the blistering heats. The soil is also,
always moist under tobacco plants, and
the thorough working necessary to secure
the largest crop puts the soil in condition
to absorb all the fertilizing gases of the at-
mosphere.

taken from communication to the Press,
are true to the letter:

1. The general idea that it is exhaustive
to the soil is false in theory, false in fact,
and utterly undeniable in every point of
view. We lay down four propositions,
which defy competition:

1. Its cultivation puts the soil in bet-
ter condition for succeeding crop than any
other plant, as is proven by the fact that
you make larger yield of wheat and get a
more perfect stand of grass after tobacco
crop than any other.

2. It feeds more from the atmosphere
after it has attained certain growth than
any plant ordinarily cultivated.

3. Its close cultivation more effectually
eradicates weeds and foul vegetation than
any other crop.

4. Its continued cultivation (indiscriminately)
year after year, on the same lots, has
far less tendency to exhaust the soil than
Indian corn, oats, sorghum, buckwheat,
barley, or timothy, cultivated in the same
manner.

Counsel at Law of said court. The complaint charges violations of his official oath, and that he did not possess good moral character. Case in progress of hearing when the hour of adjournment arrived and continued till Thursday for further hearing.

In support of the charge that he had violated his official oath by false and groundless and unlawful suits, is cited where it is claimed that in the month of February 1876 Celesia C. Skillings of Portland furnished said Proctor the sum of $14 to be paid Ashbury Libby. Proctor afterwards obtained assignment of Libby, although he had the money to pay the bill. Skillings brought suit against Proctor for the $14 which he claimed he had paid Libby for her, and obtained judgment against him. It is also claimed that the 28th of July 1871 he, having obtained the said Libby's books containing charges made by him to said Skillings, all of which had been paid and settled, including assignment, and many others which Skillings had paid directly to Libby, he brought suit in Libby's name against Skillings on account annexed, which account had been paid, as Proctor well knew, Proctor bringing the suit without Libby's knowledge, request or consent.

On the charge that he had not conducted himself with fidelity to the courts it was claimed that on August 6, 1877, at court in Bridgton, held by W. W. Cross, trial justice, Proctor attempted surreptitiously from the files of said court a certain plea of the general issue which had been filed in a then pending before said trial justice for the purpose of availing himself of the point that plea had been filed. On the same occasion he moved to dismiss an action in which he appeared as counsel for defendant, on the ground that the summons in said case was not sealed when matter of fact the seal had been removed therefrom by said Proctor after the service of said summons and before the return day of the writ.

It is also claimed that November 18th, 1871, he brought suit an attorney to enforce lien upon real estate for material furnished and labor performed, the writ being returnable to the Municipal Court of Portland. November 26th. The said writ was placed for service in the hands of Matthew Adams, city constable, who served the writ, and made his return thereon that before the return day of the writ Proctor obtained possession of the same, and before entry and after service, materially altered by adding thereto another defendant, one William Somers, and making other changes.

On the charge that he had not conducted himself with fidelity to his clients, it is claimed that in March, 1877, by false pretences he obtained the signature of one Ann N. J. Haskell to bill of sale of the household goods and other chattels to Ida M. Proctor his wife. This case has been fully reported in this paper.

Lastly it is claimed that as he has been repeatedly guilty of dishonest acts he does not possess good moral character.

In answer to these charges Mr. Proctor said that in the suit of Libby Skillings, the claim was assigned to him with right to sue and collect in his name. He transferred it to another person whom owned it when the suit was brought. Skillings did not furnish money to pay said claim, and the suit was commenced in good faith.

He makes general denial of the other charges and claims that he has never been guilty of dishonest act knowingly, or obtained goods by false pretence, or violated his official oath, and has always acted in good faith.

WASHINGTON, March 11.—Mr. Hewitt made to-day speech such as is rarely heard in either chamber upon the presentation of an appropriation bill. Speeches upon such bills are either defense of increment or an apology for extravaganza. Mr. Hewitt was neither. He dealt with the Diplomatic and Consular bill upon a higher ground, commanding the attention of the House by his comprehension of the subject he was treating. His constitutional argument was clear and logical. If it was not perfectly satisfactory to men who place a different value upon the corrective powers of the House over the expenditure of money, and in dealing with the acts of any branch of the Government, Mr. Hewitt restricted the House to purely advisory functions concerning the diplomatic intercourse of the federation. His analysis of the negotiations of the Federal Government gave historical demonstration of his assertion that special commissioners were uniformly used instead of ministers, whose function he limited to a different class of questions not now satisfactorily discharged by them. It is a very common practice for Congressmen to cut out of works, easily accessible, points which they turn to their own speeches without word of credit. It is extremely unusual for a Congressman to illustrate his speech like Hewitt did in dealing with the Consular service to-day, by adding "elaborate analysis on the Consular affairs in our country" and has shown that our diplomacy fails to gain the commercial treaties, though he also showed that the consular service is now laid a tax upon instead of being simply an aid to American commerce.

By an odds the most interesting part of Mr. Hewitt's long speech was his analysis of Mr. Hayes, whose only motive he found in the selfish purpose of rewarding neither party friends nor past associates, but his assistants and co-workers in the completion of his impudent title, which began in forgery and ended in barter. It was for this Hayes was chosen. Stoughton sent to Russia, Kasson placed in Vienna, four men sent to similar offices in Louisiana, and such Southerners rewarded as received office in his hands; it was for this he had abandoned the Blanfords, the Camerons and the Chamberlains, broken the pledges of the platform on which he was nominated, and forgotten his own promises on the assumption of an office to which he was never entitled.

More significant than Hewitt's attack upon Mr. Hayes was his remark that he hopes time would be given for a defence, when any defence was attempted, in the Republican caucus of the House. It had been expected that such defence would be made by Mr. Cox of Ohio, but it is understood that Cox has decided not to come to the aid of Hayes.

DR. HEWCOPT.

The Rev. Dr. Hopworth preached yesterday on "a Personal God," selecting for his text Exodus, vi, 5—VIII take you to men people, and will do to you = God." On a beautiful October evening, said Mr. Hopworth, in the year 1852 in his home in Marshfield, Daniel Webster lay dying. The shadows of the last change were fleeting him, and he faced the enemy who, until Christ's advent, sufficed in pressing all under his lee. When asked concerning his religious belief his eye burned for a moment and his voice, only too soon to be silenced forever, answered in no uncertain or unhesitating tones:—"There is a God; all must acknowledge Him. I see in His wondrous works both Himself and His power." Before he kissed the hills the next morning and beheld by an aroused world now day for work, Daniel Webster had closed his eyes and solved the great problem that we must ill later solve. Let me sketch another picture. Mr. Eckel is one of the foremost physicists of Germany. The dream of his life has been to account for the existence of the universe without being compelled to the result that the idea of God is necessity most natural and easy to account for its present unknown intelligence, but Eckel says, in language which seems like music in the minor key to us, that however despondingly we may take such a step, no man may at least make the attempt to undertake the existence of the world without the postulate of a ruling and supreme intelligence. The one end and aim of his life is to deny God—to account the world on purely physical grounds. God to him is unnecessary. Rather do Daniel Webster, dying in Marshfield, with the name of the one and the infinite Father on my lips amid shadows, cropping my way month after month, year after year, without ray of light to shine upon my path and without pulse of relief on my conscience. Brethren, let me say to you this morning that the best scientists that Daniel Webster right and that Eckel is wrong. If there is one emphatic word which comes from scientific men in the declaration of a personal God, supreme intelligence, supreme Benevolence that puts its everlasting arms under these frames, leads up through the darkness of persistent doubt to light of the perfect day of trust and confidence.

NO CONCESSION.

Remember, please, that no concession to the religious sentiment of mankind. Science though highly apostolic whenever science, to-day, says that outside the physical universe there is a controlling personal God to whom you can hold intimate relations, that declaration is the result of the deepest thinking of the largest knowledge of the facts and of the severest deduction therefrom. Dr. Hopworth then proceeded to describe the effect upon thinking man of a survey of the universe, how suggestive such survey was of thought—the stars in constant motion, the heart of man that beats with thrill at the spectacle of beauty—how grand everything was, and how manifest to the beholder was the fact that everything was going toward an ordained planner outside the plan or the machinery. To the demonstration of a personal God two things must be preliminarily settled. FIRST, that there was no such thing as chance. Chance was the bugbear of small mind. What seemed to be chance was really hidden law. The second thing was that matter had no power to move of itself. The best scientists of the day insist upon that in matter itself there is no power of motion. If matter moves then something moves it, and if it moves according to plan and in direction of a divine purpose then there must be a person who is strong and wise outside of all matter, and who directs and controls it. This was an assertion that was the cornerstone of the superstructure for the building of our character. The Bible is full of the declarations of a personal God. When Christ came He told us that God was not only a person, but that He was our Father, and that the bond between us was very peculiar. That was the central thought of the revelation of Jesus Christ. He had not only given us a revelation, but He had given us a pattern to follow in the life of Jesus Christ.

jury to-day. The crowd on the
street is small to-day, and no dis
order has occurred thus far.


The weather is cloudy; wind
northeast.


A Swede, named William Parson,
aged so years, shot himself in the
head yesterday at 500 Jackson
street, and died from the effects of
the wound. He left a letter saying
that he proposed to kill himself,
because he wanted rest.


The Legislature's Proceedings.
SACRAMENTO, Jan. 19.-SENATE
"A new bill was introduced by
Dean, amending section 1882 of the
Political Code by the removal of
taxation on manufactured products
of wheat. Referred to Committee
on Agriculture.


By Murphy, of San Luis Obispo
Extending the time for construc-
tion of railroad from Santa Maria
Valley to San Luis Obispo. Rules
suspended and bill finally passed.
The Riot Bill Signed.
SACRAMENTO, Jan. 10.-Governor
Irwin, after long consultation
with the Attorney General, Dis
trict Attorney Murphy and Sena-
tor Pearson, has signed the riot
bill.


The Storm Cleared Up.


KEBBELLAH, Cal, Jan. 10--
The heavy wind and rain storm
that has prevailed during the past
five days is apparently over for the
present. Streams that have over
flowed their banks are rapidly sub
siding. Communication with the
country north of here has been en-
tirely cut off by swollen streams
and washed-out roads and trails.
The weather to-day is warm and
clear. Grass is growing and grain
doing splendidly.


Weather at Mendocino.


MENDOCINO, Jan 19.-The weather
has at last cleared off. We had
a heavy storm all week. Commu.
nication has been stopped and
wires have been down. The total
rainfall from January 7th to 18th is
9.54- 100 inches. All the coast mills
have received their logs and will
commence sawing soon. The water
has been higher in the rivers this
time than for years past. Bridges
have been carried away, roads cut
up and travel stopped.


William Paddock, of Cottoneva,
well known on the coast, was
found drowned in Gordon Creek
Thursday.


The steamer Monterey could not
make landing until Thursday,
two days behind time.


The North Pacific telegraph line
has been badly demolished.


How an Investigation was Cav.
Quoted.


NEW YORK, Jan. 19th.-The
Tribune's dispatch from Washing
ton describes the features of the
recent investigation into the Ind.
ian Bureau, of which ex-Com-
missioner Smith and Chief Clerk
Galpin complain. It appears that
the accused men were not allowed
to answer the charges brought
against them, nor to be heard in
their own defense, Galpin being
forbidden, in fact, to enter the De-
partment. Yet the Board of In
quiry complained that it was as-
sisted in the investigation by these
officials. Members of the Board
were prejudiced in advance, and
the conclusions they came to after
a secret inquiry were published to
the world without being accompa-
nied by the defense of Galpin and
Smith. A letter has also been re-
ceived from President Seelye show
ing the unfairness with which
Galpin was treated.


Sea Land Claim Determined.


WASHINGTON, Dec. 19.-The
Secretary of the Interior has rem
dered a decision in the case of the
State of California VS. M. d. Town
send, et al, involving the right to
certain lands in township 3 south,
range 3 east, Mount Diablo Meri-
dian, San Francisco, District of
California, on appeal from decision
of Commissioner of General Land
Office of Nov. 15th, 1876. The State
claims the land by virtue of certain
invalid indemnity school selections,
which, it is alleged, were conferred
by act of Congress, approved July
23d, 1866, entitled An Act to
quiet land titles in California.
Certain persons claim title
as bona fide settlers under
presumption laws, and the Western
Pacific Railroad claims the odd Sec
tions by virtue of the grant to aid
in the construction of said road.
The whole subject is considered at
length by the Secretary, who de-
cides that the even sections of the
lands in dispute outside of the
Lewis survey (several surveys are
involved in the case) are awarded
to the State and the odd sections to
the Railroad Company. The par
ties claiming under pre-emption
laws are thrown out, because it
is shown that none of the
lands in question were pre-
empted prior to their withdrawal
for railroad purposes. The Com
missioner is instructed to comply.

From the Ohio Statesman, Dec. 7.


About the first of June last, we recorded
the incorporation of a new institution, The
State Mutual Aid Association, an insur-
ance association based on the mutual assess-
ment plan.


Since that date we have almost lost sight
of this enterprise, so quietly and smoothly
has it done its work. A few days ago we
visited the Home Office and found the Pres-
ident, Hon. WIN. BELL Jr., the Secretary,
J. H. SAMPSON, and the assistant, busy
attending to the duties of their offices, and
almost hidden under the immense pile of
applications before them, and issuing cir-
tificates, answering letters, sending out sup-
plies, etc. Upon inquiry we found already
upon their books nearly 600 members, from
every part of Ohio. Taking into consider-
ation the fact that this Association has been
actively at work only six months, and the
fact that during much of July and August,
business of all kinds was suspended for har-
vest and the great strike, the growth of this
Association has been remarkable. The
causes which have led to such encouraging
results are the peculiarly clear, equitable
and popular plan of giving both life and
endowment insurance at cost, and allowing
the members to control their own money
and use it until actually needed to pay
losses. A member of this Association does


not have to pay out large amounts of


money to be squandered by extrava-
gance, nor do they have to pay their insur-
ance during their whole life to secure the
benefit. Those who remain faithful to the
Association from 15 to 25 years receive
themselves, all the benefits of their insur-
ance. Some of the features so popular with
this Association, are:


1st. Endowment Insurance on the Mu-
tual Assessment plan.


2d. Uniform membership fee only $15 for any age or amount taken.


3d. No annual dues, or other extra char-
ges, whatever.


4th. Return of all assessments paid in al-
l to date of claim pro rata, to the number of
certificates in force at that date.


5th. No division into classes.


6th. Care in selection of risks, and strict
economy in its management.


7th. Charging the members for insur-
ance according to what they get.


The fact that they have as yet not had
loss, and are rapidly approaching large
membership, shows that the plan is not an
experiment, and that good insurance can
be had at home, where all the officers are
known, and all the money kept within one's
own State.


The officers are men of integrity and en-
ergy, and we have this to say of our own
confidence in them and their plan, that we
have taken membership in the associ-
ation, and would heartily recommend to
friends to do likewise.


Their Home office is in Rooms 2 and
Capital Block, near the New York Store.


P.S. Since the above was published, its
membership has reached nearly 900, and
the Association has had one death.
